findings.claim: Flashcard [5] asks 'What Victorian-era science inspired Shelley's reanimation idea?' (answer: galvanism).
findings.truth: Galvani's experiments date from the 1780s-90s and the novel was published in 1818. Victoria came to the throne in 1837, so nothing in Frankenstein is Victorian. Calling the context Victorian is a standard AO3 error that examiners penalise.
findings.evidence: Novel published 1 January 1818; Galvani's frog experiments 1780s. Spec AO3 (specs/aqa/english-literature-8702-8702.md, line 553) asks for the context in which the text was written.

findings.claim: Printed extract reads 'So much has been done - far more will I achieve: treading in the steps already marked...'
findings.truth: The novel reads 'So much has been done, exclaimed the soul of Frankenstein-more, far more, will I achieve; treading in the steps already marked...'. An extract printed for the student to analyse must be verbatim.

findings.claim: 'In her 1831 preface, she described conversations between Percy Shelley and Byron...'
findings.truth: The 1831 piece is titled 'Introduction'. The 1818 Preface was written by Percy Shelley. The quoted phrases ('the nature of the principle of life', 're-animated') are correct and come from the 1831 Introduction. Not worth a narration re-record for one word.
findings.evidence: Mary Shelley, Introduction to the 1831 edition (not in the Gutenberg body text used here).

findings.claim: 'tabula rasa' is defined as 'the philosophical idea (associated with Rousseau) that humans are born good'; the conclusion says 'Rousseau's tabula rasa'; flashcard [5] says 'Tabula rasa - from Rousseau's philosophy.'
findings.truth: Tabula rasa (blank slate) is John Locke's term, from An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1689). Rousseau's contribution is natural goodness corrupted by society, which the lesson states correctly elsewhere. The gloss also defined the wrong idea.
findings.evidence: Locke, Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Book II. Rousseau, Emile (1762) / Discourse on Inequality (1755).

findings.claim: Victor's nightmare: his mother's corpse, 'shrouded in a flannel.'
findings.truth: Not a quotation from the novel. The text reads 'a shroud enveloped her form, and I saw the grave-worms crawling in the folds of the flannel.'

findings.claim: The Creature 'might have been the "new Adam" it later describes itself as'; flashcard [12] answers "'New Adam' - then the 'fallen angel' after rejection."
findings.truth: 'New Adam' does not appear anywhere in the novel. The Creature says 'I ought to be thy Adam, but I am rather the fallen angel, whom thou drivest from joy for no misdeed.'
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #84 (1831 text) scripts/_retrofc/_texts/frankenstein.txt lines 3054-3056 (ch. 10); grep for 'new adam' returns nothing.

findings.claim: The lesson places the Creature's reading of Victor's journal after the De Lacey rejection, and the Key Fact lists it as cause (4), after the beating.
findings.truth: The Creature finds and reads the journal in the hovel earlier in chapter 15; it approaches the blind De Lacey later in the same chapter and declares 'everlasting war' in chapter 16. The lesson reverses the order, which would cost AO1 structure marks.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #84 (1831 text) scripts/_retrofc/_texts/frankenstein.txt journal at line 4086, De Lacey approach at line 4196, 'everlasting war' at line 4325 (ch. 15 begins 3989, ch. 16 begins 4298).

findings.claim: Flashcard [4] asks 'Which quote shows the Creature echoing Milton's Adam against Victor?' and answers with 'Did I request thee, Maker, from my clay to mould me man?'
findings.truth: That line is Milton's Adam (Paradise Lost X.743-45), used by Shelley as the title-page epigraph. The Creature never speaks it. The lesson body labels it correctly as the epigraph; only the flashcard mis-frames it.
findings.evidence: 1818/1831 title-page epigraph; grep for 'request thee' in Gutenberg #84 (1831 text) scripts/_retrofc/_texts/frankenstein.txt returns nothing.

findings.claim: 'Felix teaches Safie (a Turkish woman) to read using Volney's Ruins of Empires'.
findings.truth: Safie is the daughter of a Turkish merchant, but her mother was 'a Christian Arab' and Shelley consistently calls her 'the Arabian'. 'Turkish merchant's daughter' would be more accurate. Not mark-affecting, so not worth a narration re-record.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #84 (1831 text) scripts/_retrofc/_texts/frankenstein.txt lines 3713 (Volney), 3822-3823 (Turkish merchant), 3869 (Christian Arab mother), 3666 ff. ('the Arabian').

findings.claim: 'Victor describes his guilt: "The blood of the murdered one was not more terrible to me than the anguish of the living victim of my machinations."'
findings.truth: Fabricated quotation - the sentence is not in the novel. The real line at that point is 'But I, the true murderer, felt the never-dying worm alive in my bosom.' Students memorising the invented line would lose AO1 credit for inaccurate reference.
findings.evidence: grep 'machinations' in Gutenberg #84 (1831 text) scripts/_retrofc/_texts/frankenstein.txt returns only lines 4942, 5733, 6072, none matching. Real line at 2650 (ch. 8).

findings.claim: Practice question 2 mark scheme: 'AO3 (6): Links to Victorian attitudes to women, coerced confessions, and Shelley's moral purpose.'
findings.truth: Frankenstein is 1818, two decades before Victoria. The mark scheme tells the student to write anachronistic context on the one AO worth 6 marks.
findings.evidence: Publication 1 January 1818; Victoria acceded 1837. Spec AO3 (line 553).

findings.claim: 'The Creature watches through the window, "a grin on its face"' (repeated in flashcard [3]).
findings.truth: The text reads 'A grin was on the face of the monster; he seemed to jeer, as with his fiendish finger he pointed towards the corpse of my wife.'

findings.claim: Quotation bank Key Fact and flashcard [0] both give 'So much has been done - far more will I achieve.'
findings.truth: The novel reads 'So much has been done, exclaimed the soul of Frankenstein-more, far more, will I achieve'. This is a memorisation list, so the wording must be exact.

findings.claim: Flashcard [4] asks 'Which Miltonic line does the Creature quote to challenge Victor?' and answers with the epigraph.
findings.truth: Same error as F8. The line is Shelley's title-page epigraph from Paradise Lost, not the Creature's speech. The lesson body (n8) already calls it the epigraph.
findings.evidence: Title-page epigraph, Paradise Lost X.743-45; not in the novel's text.

findings.claim: In lessons 2-6 every practice question stores literal backslash-n characters instead of newlines, e.g. 'Read the following extract:\\n\\n\u201cA new species...'. Lesson 1 and lesson 7 store real newlines.
findings.truth: Students see the characters \\n printed on screen in 30 practice questions across five lessons. It is a storage defect, not a fact error, and it almost certainly affects other English Literature units built by the same generator. Options: (a) fix here as part of this unit's edits, (b) sweep every unit's practice_questions with one script. Recommend (b) - a corpus-wide sweep - because a per-unit fix leaves the same defect everywhere else.
findings.evidence: scripts/_retrofc/units/english-literature-aqa__frankenstein/_raw.json: lessons 2-6 practice_questions[*].text and .marks contain the two-character sequence backslash + n.

summary: Seven lessons checked against the 1831 Gutenberg text and AQA 8702. Three HIGH errors: a fabricated Victor quotation in L5, and two Victorian-era context claims about an 1818 novel (L1 flashcard, L5 AO3 mark scheme). Nine further quotation, attribution and plot-order fixes; exam claims (Paper 1 Section B, 30 marks, AO1 12 / AO2 12 / AO3 6, no SPaG) are all correct. Lesson 2 is factually clean; F15 is a rendering defect spanning lessons 2-6.
